newsitem.title: LATVIA: ESTONIA-FINNISH REPORT OPTIMISTIC ON GROWTH, INFLATION.
newsitem.headline: ESTONIA-FINNISH REPORT OPTIMISTIC ON GROWTH, INFLATION.

text.p: Estonia's economy should enjoy good growth rates despite a limited resource base until the end of the century, a report released by the Research Institute of the Finnish Economy (ETLA) said on Friday.
The report, The Estonian Economy and European Integration, sees rising growth rates, lower inflation and an improvement in macroeconomic conditions to the end of the century.

But it notes that a number of structural and microeconomic issues still need to be addressed and warns that the country's commitment to a balanced budget could be derailed at the end of the decade when state and government guaranteed loans are due.

"The rate of inflation is expected to slow down and remain below ten percent annually starting from 1998," the report, which was prepared in cooperation with the Estonian Institute of Economics, said.
In the short-term, it said that prices in the non-tradeable sector were expected to rise. But it said that prices in the tradeable sector were approaching world market levels.
The report was bullish on the country's growth prospects.
It forecast gross domestic product (GDP) growth of four to five percent in 1997, five to 6.5 percent in 1998, and a tigerish expansion of 7.5 to 8 percent in the year 2000.
It also predicted that the structure of the country's GDP would continue to change as it completed its transition to a market economy.

The report forecasts that farming, hunting and forestry would continue contribute less to the country's overall economy and be attributable for just 5.9 percent of GDP in 2000 compared to 8.4 percent in 1995.
Manufarcturing will account for 17.6 percent of GDP in 2000 compared to 16.9 percent in 1995, ETLA forecast.
The report said that the growth in manufacturing will be spurred by investments, which have lagged somewhat to date, and structural changes in the sector.

But it predicted that the expansion wholsesale and retail trade will slow as the sector has grown faster than purchasing power and as higher prices make the country a less attractive tourist destination.

It added that Estonia's geographical position and expected improvements in the country's infrustructure would spark faster growth in transport, storage and communications, which it predicted would account for 11.8 percent of GDP in 2000 compared to 10.6 percent in 1995.
"The repayment of loans taken and guaranteed by the Estonian government will begin 1998, and this may endanger the balanced budget at the turn of the century," the report said.
But it noted that Estonia's debt burden was low for an economy in transition.
On the micro side, it said that direct investments and foreign loans to industry have been too low to date.
It said that most investments and loans have been channeled "in activities with fast turnover such as banking."
"The share of enterprises' equity capital has been low in investment (because of) the relatively low profitability of enterprises' economic activity," it said.
It also noted that the labour market, which has been characterized by a decline in the share of the working age population, could be a cause for conern.
